elements.text: Flightcrew's failure to maintain required minimum descent altitude until visual references were in sight
BDL approach controller's failure to furnish the flightcrew with a current altimeter setting
Flightcrew's failure to ask for a more current altimeter setting
Flightcrew had proper FAA airmen certifications and were qualified
Flightcrew received proper crew rest and were not under unusual psychological pressure
Airplane was properly fueled and loaded in accordance with requirements
Flight was released in accordance with dispatch procedures
Weather at BDL was at or above required minimums with overcast clouds, rain, and wind
No evidence of malfunction in pitot-static, autopilot, GPWS, windshear warning, or flight control systems
AAL weather forecasts (SIGMECs) were substantially correct
AAL's system of providing SIGMECs is a valid method of weather dissemination
Atmospheric pressure decrease was not underestimated by the flight data recorder
Flightcrew had adequate weather information except for a current altimeter setting
Flightcrew should have requested a current altimeter setting due to rapidly falling pressure
Receiving a current altimeter setting at 0043 likely would have resulted in the aircraft being 40 feet higher
Indicated altitude was about 76 feet too high due to the altimeter setting received at 0030
Not using the most current QNH setting in the standby altimeter did not affect the accident sequence
First officer monitoring instruments until MDA would have helped notice altitude deviation
Excellent crew resource management limited passenger injuries
FAA quality control was inadequate for resolving tree height on the ridge line
Value in flying non-precision approaches with constant rate or angle of descent
FAA did not consider precipitous terrain when developing the approach to runway 15
Ridge line on final approach course is an obstacle that should be depicted on charts
It would have been prudent for the controller to issue altimeter setting changes as the airplane neared the airport
Closure of the tower was a good managerial decision due to safety concerns
TRACON supervisor's communications were appropriate and aided the flightcrew
ATIS broadcast should have been updated to reflect tower closure
MSAW operated properly despite lack of full coverage
Tower controller being relieved should have advised that ATIS needed updating
Variable wind conditions did not cause large-scale updrafts or downdrafts affecting the aircraft
Decreasing headwind shear was not significant
Weather was not severe enough to cause deviation below MDA
Three to 6 months to verify LLWAS sensor alignment is unacceptable
Misaligned LLWAS wind sensor did not contribute to the accident
Ambiguous instructions in Douglas Maintenance Manual could lead to misrigging emergency evacuation slides
Douglas uses different terms for the same part in maintenance manuals, causing confusion
Directing passengers to remove shoes during evacuations may not be in the best interests of safety
